newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine's reforms finely poised as Lazarenko exits.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine's reforms finely poised as Lazarenko exits.

text.p: President Leonid Kuchma has shaken off a reform-shy prime minister by accepting Pavlo Lazarenko's resignation, but the benefits for Ukraine remain to be seen and the jilted premier may yet stage a comeback.
Many political analysts predict an end-of-the-century clash of the Titans following Lazarenko's departure from the premiership of a young country that is the third biggest recipient of U.S. aid.
Kuchma and Lazarenko are widely expected to compete in a presidential election in 1999. Both are from Dnipropetrovsk, the richest region in Europe's second biggest country.
Lazarenko's departure comes at a delicate stage of reforms in the former Soviet republic.
"If he is replaced by a committed reformer then it could make a difference, if that were accompanied by real reforms in the government structure," one political analyst said.
"It's an opening, but it remains to be seen whether it will be used the right way," he added.
Ukraine has achieved a stable hryvnia currency, while inflation this year is forecast at less than 10 percent from 10,000 percent in 1993 and 181 percent in 1995.
It is hoping for its first growth in gross domestic product this year after it fell by 10 percent last year.

But Ukraine has struggled with privatisation, whose snail's pace is partly blamed on Lazarenko, and it needs to make structural reforms in government, the agricultural sector and in the monopolistic energy sector to qualify for more loans from the International Monetary Fund.
A dozen potential candidates have been mentioned in parliament's corridors since Lazarenko's resignation, but no clear favourite had emerged by Friday.

Arch-reformers like Viktor Yushchenko, who has steered the central bank since 1993, could get a cool reception in the conservative-dominated parliament, which must approve any candidate by a majority.
Kuchma said he would try to propose a candidate quickly but his chief-of-staff said he could wait until parliament, due to shut down for summer in mid-July, reconvenes in September.

Whoever he chooses as his new prime minister, the president appeared to make political capital out of Lazarenko's departure on Thursday when he said he had "no doubt" Ukraine would enter phase two of the IMF's lending programme.
The Fund had said recently it might delay a three-year, $2.5-$3 billion loan meant for countries undertaking structural reforms and issue an interim stand-by deal in the meantime.

Kuchma was also quick to point out that U.S. Vice President Al Gore had called him during a regional summit in southwest Ukraine to say Washington still considered Ukraine a strategic partner and that it would take this into account in its actions.
Kuchma had said right after signing his 44-year-old colleague's resignation on health grounds on Wednesday that reforms would be accelerated.
In their native Dnipropetrovsk, Kuchma -- who once ran the Soviet Union's biggest missile plant there -- is seen as a weaker figure than Lazarenko, who was elected the region's governor in 1994.
But overall, the president has considerable advantages.

Lazarenko, a heavy, imposing man who rarely smiles and lacks Kuchma's slickness, could find himself turning to the left for his political base now that his unaffiliated status has gone, analysts said.

Lazarenko, who rose from farm driver to manager to politician, has denied allegations that he has a stake in the country's main gas supplier, United Energy Systems of Ukraine, and that he earned $200 million in revenues from it.
Some analysts say Lazarenko's admission to hospital on June 19 was negotiated with Kuchma as a way for him to leave the premiership without losing face. Few believe he is actually ill.

Further complicating this back-stage manoeuvring, Kuchma said last week he might extend parliament's term by one year to give it more time to approve reforms instead of getting caught up in election campaigning.

Few accepted Kuchma's idea that reforms will speed up, saying it would all make little difference to a country which took six months to pass this year's budget and where requests for bribes from badly-paid officials are a fact of life.
